en: Now begins the first chapter of the Kapila Purāṇa:
May those [arms] which are dark as rain-clouds and hardened by the striking of the bowstring of the Śārṅga protect you!
The four arms of Hari are the pillars for the pavilion of the three worlds. ||1||
Śalyajit said:
"I have heard of the sacred fields that remove sins;
now I wish to hear about the fields in the land of Utkala. (2)
Tell me all of those fields, whatever merit they possess, whatever sacred fords and deities reside there, and whatever supports they have—those who are worthy of honor. (3)
"O great sage, through your grace I shall have my purpose fulfilled;
O Lord, you are worthy of salutation and most deserving of worship by all the deities. (4)
For you indeed know all the eighteen Purāṇas; you know all the Śāstras; you are omniscient, O great sage! (5)
Kapila said:
O King, listen with a one-pointed mind as I tell you a secret, by the mere remembrance of which all impurities indeed go to their destruction. (6)
Among the regions of the Varṣas, Bhārata is the best; among countries, Utkala is remembered as such. There is no country on the surface of the earth equal to Utkala. (7)
In this very context, they cite this ancient history, a dialogue between the sages and the wise Bhāradvāja.
And while staying in the holy Puṣkara forest, all those preeminent sages, their sins destroyed, spoke thus to Bharadvāja: ||9||
The sages said:
O learned one, tell us all that merit is proclaimed to exist in that holy forest, as well as whatever is to be experienced by those who have committed sins.
Bharadvāja said:
O brahmins, those best of men who dwell in this meritorious forest—their great fortune and their fruitful birth are extolled by the twice-born. (11)
O brahmins, those people who worship Janārdana in this Puṣkara forest shall attain the abode of Hari after effecting the destruction of all their sins. ||12||
In this place, for those fortunate ones who are free from passion and devoid of blemish and who desire to dwell here, it is heard that the lives of their parents have become fruitful. (13)
Those who bestow gifts here upon the twice-born with great devotion reach the heavenly world and never leave it.
O ascetics, even very little merit here becomes manifold;
even the gods desire to dwell here—what need is there to mention others, O twice-born ones? (15)
Those who sleep here, those people who bow to Janārdana, those who take their meals here, and those who worship Maheśvara; ||16||
O ascetics rich in penance, the best of men, having cast off their lives here at this Puṣkara which possesses such qualities as these, have gone to heaven. (17)
This most meritorious sacred ford is renowned as the best among forests; it is frequented by the gods and praised by those at holy watering places.
It was exceedingly beautified by *vakula*, *campaka*, *vakra*, and *dāḍima* trees, as well as by *aśoka*, *punnāga*, *karṇikāra*, and *pāṭala* trees. ||19||
With clusters of *pānasa* trees, coconut palms, and date palms;
with *sāla*, *tāla*, and *tamāla* trees, as well as *vaṭa* and *aśvattha* trees. ||20||
Thus, it was filled on all sides with various kinds of trees, joined with jasmine and *jātī* flowers, and beautified by *kunda* blossoms. ||21||
This sacred [thread], joined with *tulasī* leaves, is the destroyer of sin;
yet those men who, possessed by delusion, commit sin here— ||22||
For them, however, there shall indeed be no rebirth in this best of lands, Bhārata;
for here, even that which is as small as an atom may indeed become like a mountain.
In this place, accepting a gift is terrible, like the hālāhala poison; even the merit that exists in other fields shall here come to destruction. ||24||
O Brahmins, even a slight sin committed here becomes equal to Mount Meru; for this reason, O twice-born ones, if you desire the supreme goal, [you must act accordingly].
"Abandoning all evils, perform meritorious deeds there.
Having heard these words of his, the sages, longing for merit, [acted accordingly]. ||26||
The sages spoke these great words, deep and resonant as thunderclouds, to Bhāradvāja:
"O high-minded Bhāradvāja, that merit there is indeed difficult to perform."
"O Lord, tell us that place where even sin becomes most meritorious.
Bharadvāja said:
"O twice-born ones, in the past, when I asked about this matter, Kuśaketu [replied]:"
When he said, "Listen to that which liberates from the evils of existence:
there is one preeminent region among all lands, the highly renowned land of Oḍra," [29]
O scorcher of enemies, even sins become meritorious in that land;
there are sacred fields, holy fords, and great seers present there.
There, even a small amount of merit becomes exceedingly great; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, O Brahmins, this sacred field should be resorted to with diligent effort. (31)
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Question of the Sages," in the glorious Kapila Purāṇa. ||1||
Now begins the second chapter.
The sages said:
"Relate in detail the majesty of the land of Oḍra."
To that region where we shall go, we shall remain as its inhabitants.
Bharadvāja said:
O twice-born ones, listen as I describe in detail the land of Oḍhra, ordained by the gods and which removes all sins. (2)
In that Oḍra, Kṛṣṇa, Arka, Pārvatī, and Hara are always present;
thus, this sacred field of Īśa is the destroyer of all sins. ||3||
In that region, O best of the twice-born, there is a most excellent river among rivers, renowned as Mahānadī, which removes all sins. ||4||
I shall describe the majesty of that river again and again:
having bathed in it, the best of men attains the divine world. ||5||
Formerly, in the Tretā Yuga, there was a renowned Brāhmaṇa named Sukānti, the son of Pulaha, who was a scholar of all the scriptures and an expert in ethics.
Standing on Mount Mahendra, that twice-born one, Sukānti, spoke to his father: "O Lord, this place has indeed become crowded with people. (7)
"Tell me, let me go to the great forest to practice asceticism.
Pulaha said: "It is abandoned by all beings and brings happiness to all birds. (8)
It was filled with many deer, frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas, and celebrated by the wise as a great place for asceticism. (9)
"Go with a joyful heart to the fruitful Vindhya mountain.
Having heard these words of his father, Sukānti departed immediately. (10)
The wise, having gone to that great, solitary place which yields the fruit of all merits, bestows auspiciousness, and is fit for asceticism, beheld it for the sake of penance.
Having reflected thus in his mind, "I shall perform penance here," he performed penance for the sake of water, as he did not find water there.
Come, O Goddess Nimnagā, best of rivers, beloved of the ocean;
I shall perform penance here. O Gaṅgā, show me your grace! (13)
Having recited this supreme mantra, he indeed attained all perfections through the grace of this mantra as well as the ascetic power of the brahmin. (14)
There, Gaṅgā, the remover of all sins, descended.
Gaṅgā said:
"Excellent, my son! O highly fortunate one, great penance has been performed by you."
"I came to the Vindhya mountain, the best of peaks, for your sake;
now, O Brahmin, perform great penance according to your own will. (16)
I shall remain here, however, until you have obtained the fruit of your asceticism;
thereafter, I will depart from this Vindhya range toward the eastern ocean.
Now I shall remain here for the sake of asceticism; and since I am difficult to attain even for the gods, what need is there to mention human beings? (18)
"And I have been obtained by you, O Brahmin, through the power of Pulaha.
Bharadvāja said:
"Having heard the words of Gaṅgā, the son of Pulaha was pleased in his heart."
O twice-born ones, he spoke these words, deep as a thundercloud, to the daughter of Jahnu.
You are the beloved of the Lord of Beings, the God who holds the discus in his hand;
you are indeed the beloved of Brahmā and difficult for all others to attain.
Formerly you were born from the world of Brahmā; from there, you descended onto the head of Śaṅkara, and from there you have come to dwell upon the earth for the sake of the welfare of living beings.
Having spoken thus to the Jāhnavī, that best of brahmins, standing before her with palms joined in reverence, sought her protection and offered this hymn of praise.
Sukānti said:
I bow to the Goddess Jāhnavī, the destroyer of sins and affectionate toward her devotees;
for you are the purifier of the three worlds, so protect me who have come to you for refuge. (23)
You are the destroyer of all sins and the dispeller of the suffering of all the world; you are to be worshipped by all the gods, and I bow to you again and again. ||24||
I bow to you, the source of all beings, who abide upon the head of the Lord of Girijā, and who reside within the water-pot of Brahmā as the Gaṅgā. 25.
I bow to you, O highly fortunate one, born from the lotus feet of Viṣṇu, who granted the boon to Bhagīratha and delivered the sons of Sagara. 26.
Having heard this hymn of praise, O brahmins, the highly meritorious Gaṅgā fell to the surface of the earth upon seeing the devotion of the twice-born one.
He lifted the Brahmin who had fallen to the ground with his two arms,
and having kissed him on the face, he wiped the dust from his body.
She placed him on her lap and spoke these sweet words:
Gaṅgā said, "O highly fortunate one, you are my son by dharma; there is no doubt about this. (27)
"Even now I am your mother; choose a boon, O observer of noble vows.
Sukānti said, "As was previously spoken by you, I shall go to the eastern ocean."
Go now, O Mother; may my fame indeed endure forever.
"Furthermore, I desire another boon; let it be granted to me who have sought refuge:
may my austerity, acquired through my power, become complete in that regard. (31)
Gaṅgā said:
"So be it, O illustrious one; your ascetic merit has been acquired through your power.
Yet, O best of the twice-born, I shall not attain renown here by my own name. (32)
"Bringing forth Bhagīratha, I shall always attain renown here as the 'Great River' (Mahānadī), truly destroying all sins. (33)
Therefore, it is said that my fame, which removes all sins, shall always remain here upon this earth, a hundred times more powerful than that [of the former]. 34.
Bharadvāja said:
Having thus granted him the boon, Gaṅgā, the purifier of the three worlds,
assumed a watery form and flowed toward the eastern ocean.
The great river Gaṅgā, which is of great merit, beloved by Mahādeva, and auspicious, remains having assumed a second form. ||36||
Having reached Utkaleśa, as far as the Great Goddess Citrā, there she is known by the name Citrotpalā, the bestower of all merit. ||37||
Having bathed in the Mahānadī and beheld Pārvatīhara, a man is liberated from all sins and obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā. ||38||
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Mahānadī," in the glorious Kapila Purāṇa. ||2||
Now begins the third chapter.
The sages said:
O Brahmin, you have previously described to us Kṛṣṇa, Arka, Pārvatī, and Hara.
Tell me truly of their field and their sacred ford. ||1||
Bharadvāja said:
O best of the twice-born, listen as I shall briefly proclaim first the majesty of Kṛṣṇa, and the majesty of the sacred field and the holy fords. 2.
The sacred field of Nīlācala belongs to Him who is the very embodiment of Dārubrahman;
by casting off the body in this field, a person shall attain Vaikuṇṭha. ||3||
The great and highly meritorious Nīlācala mountain, which is dear to the Giver of Boons,
extends for ten yojanas and rises to half a yojana in height.
It was crowded with various throngs of sages, graced by birds, and endowed with fruit-bearing trees as well as flowers of many kinds. ||5||
That sacred field, Śrī Puruṣottama, is the manifest form of Vaikuṇṭha itself; it is the field of all fields and the most excellent of all holy places.
Sleep, meditative absorption, virtuous deeds, supreme bliss, and liberation—all these actions and qualities are auspicious when directed toward the Supreme Person. (7)
In that field, there are always those who have taken the form of the murder of a Brahmin,
yet they behold the Lord of the World after bathing in the great ocean of sacred fords (tīrtha).
O Brahmins, in ancient times on the best of blue mountains, he bore the form of a blue stone; but now the Lord of the World shines with a body as dark as a forest of tamāla trees.
The sages said:
How was it formerly that Bharadvāja became the God of gods and Lord of the universe?
And how is it that he is now separately [known] as Nīlāśmāṅga on the Blue Mountain (Nīlādri)?
Bharadvāja said:
I shall relate that eternal narrative in brief, hearing which human beings never again fall into delusion. (11)
O brahmins, in the Satya Yuga there was a lord of the earth named Indradyumna;
he was like the moon in the Ocean of Milk and the destroyer of the families of his enemies.
O Brahmins, he whose devotion is considered firm toward the God of gods, the Lord of the universe, is himself the manifest fifth body of the Brāhmaṇa.
When the illustrious Lord Śambhu took the daughter of Himādri, he then suddenly struck off the fifth head of Brahmā. ||14||
From that time forth, O Brahmins, the four-faced Brahmā himself became known as Mahābāhu Indradyumna, whose head had been severed. ||15||

He was a performer of sacrifices, an ascetic, self-controlled, peaceful, and a worshiper of guests; he was a devotee of Viṣṇu, endowed with truthfulness, and had conquered both anger and his senses. ||16||
Thus this protector of the earth reflected in his mind:
"I shall drink Viṣṇu, the victorious one with four arms, with my two eyes."
O twice-born ones, while the protector of the earth was reflecting in this manner,
Viṣṇu appeared to him in a dream and spoke these words.
The Blessed Lord said:
O King Indradyumna, protector of the earth, listen to my beneficial words; having heard them, O observer of noble vows, you shall never again fall into delusion.
On the shore of the salt ocean, covered with sands,
there stands my field Nīlācala, which bestows liberation.
This secret place is difficult to attain; it is a ground unattainable even for Brahmā and others.
Even yogis who are free from passion do not know my abode.
O protector of the earth, this sacred field, which bestows merit and is worthy of my worship as Puruṣottama,
remains even when all moving and unmoving beings have perished at the time of universal dissolution.
In this entire world, which is indeed afflicted by suffering and submerged in the waters of compassion,
there are great fields of merit, sacred fords, and holy shrines.
O lord of the earth, having completely abandoned these delightful hermitages, Vaikuṇṭha, the Ocean of Milk, and other such excellent abodes, [he has come here].
"I am staying here within the hollow of a banyan leaf in Śrī Puruṣottama; go there with great effort and well-restrained, O protector of the earth. (25)
O Indra, after you have performed austerities, you shall indeed behold me in my blue-bodied form.
The great holy place named Rohiṇī stands right by my side; having bathed there with devotion, a person certainly merges into my body. (27)
When Keśava, the slayer of Keśin, had spoken thus,
sleep itself departed from the royal sage Indradyumna.
Then, having awakened from sleep and not seeing Śyāmasundara, the king, afflicted by intense grief, wept while crying out, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! (29)
What wrong have I done to the gods and the brahmins? While I was looking on, where has the dark-complexioned, stainless one gone? (30)
"The cows have come for water; were they restrained by me previously? Where has Hari, the bearer of the conch and discus, gone while I was looking on? (31)
The mango, nimba, kadamba, and other trees have been covered by me;
where has the yellow-robed wielder of the mace gone while I was looking on? (32)
At the time for the Vaiśvadeva offering, no guest was honored by me; while I looked on, where has the God of gods, the Lord of the world, departed? (33)
"What slander has been leveled against me? And what garment was taken by me? While I was looking on, where has he gone—he who gave delight to the daughter of the ocean? (34)
"Brahmins and cows have been slaughtered by me, even by the thousands; yet while I looked on, where has he gone—he who shares half the body with Śaṅkara? (35)
"Why were my subjects, overwhelmed by suffering, not protected quickly?
While I was looking on, where has Rāghava, the destroyer of Rāvaṇa, gone? (36)
"What does it matter to me if a clod of earth, a blade of grass, or a piece of wood thrown into a well or a reservoir has vanished from my sight?
Where has that sin gone by which the slayer of Keśin was destroyed? (37)
O members of the assembly, were you not honored at the proper time, and was no libation offered by me?
While I looked on, where has the increaser of the cowherd girls' joy gone? (38)
As the wise Indradyumna was thus lamenting,
his ministers, the citizens, and the illustrious family priests arrived.
Seeing the weeping of that king Indradyumna, they all, their minds deeply distressed, spoke these words. ||41||
The ministers said:
"O lord of the earth, O mighty-armed one, for what reason have you wept?
Tell us the truth; we shall accomplish it, of this there is no doubt. (42)
Thus further propitiated by the ministers and the domestic priests, he spoke to them with effort, in a voice faltering with joy: ||43||
Indradyumna said:
"In a dream, I beheld the Lord of the Universe, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace; wearing a garland of forest flowers and yellow garments, dark as a rain cloud, the husband of Ramā. (44)
Hṛṣīkeśa said to me, who had committed sins in a dream:
"Go, O King; after performing penance on Mount Nīla, you shall see him."
"And now I shall go to Nīlādri, which bestows purity; O ministers, quickly prepare the provisions that are agreeable to me. (46)
Having accepted [the proposal], all the citizens, ministers, and priests then entered; thereafter, the king departed, and they each went to their own city.
Bharadvāja said: In the meantime, O brahmins, Yama, the son of the Sun,
his desire thwarted at that very moment, entered Mount Nīla.
Distressed and trembling again and again, the brother of Yamunā stood before Vāsudeva and spoke these words.
Yama said:
"Salutations be unto you, Viṣṇu, whose self is the welfare of all worlds;
you are liberated from passion and darkness, O Self-luminous One, salutations be unto you. (50)
"I have been created by you, O King of the Dead, O God of gods, Lord of the universe!
What shall I do, O mighty-armed one? For you are indeed the destroyer of the distressed and the afflicted. (51)
The Blessed Lord said: "What sorrow has arisen for you? Tell me before me;
I shall cut away that sorrow, O son of the Sun, in truth. (52)
Yama said:
"O Lord, you have made true your word; now I shall speak it.
Act accordingly, O mighty-armed one; listen, O Madhusūdana. (53)
"King Indradyumna is approaching with his army;
they will all attain liberation. Tell me, O Lord, what shall I do? (53)
O Keśava, having abandoned Jagannātha, who has the hue of a blue sapphire and a dark-blue body, let that sacred ford named Rohi go to the netherworld! 54.
O mighty-armed one, having bathed in which even a crow attained liberation, and upon beholding whose form even a corpse became free from old age and death. (56)
The Blessed Lord said:
"What you have previously spoken is true; what shall I do now?
O Bhāskara, let all the words that you have spoken come to pass exactly so."
Then Viśvakarman quickly fashioned the pair of images.
Bharadvāja said:
Having received the command from the Lord of the World, the Sun-god went to his own abode.
Even the Blessed One, the God of gods, does not reside on the auspicious Nīlācala mountain. ||58||
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Bestowal of Boons upon Yama," in the glorious Kapila Purāṇa. ||3||
Now begins the fourth chapter:
On the Blue Mountain (Nīlaśaila), the lord of the earth, together with his ministers, priests, experts in the Purāṇas, his subjects, and his elephants, [sought] Jagannātha. ||1||
Then, while traveling on the road, he saw Śirottama at the edge of a forest;
having worshipped and bowed to them, he went to Mount Nīla. ||2||
Beyond Svarṇakūṭa, the Blue Mountain indeed shines resplendent upon the earth;
having arrived there, he beheld the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace.
Having approached him, that king, with a dejected mind, joined his palms in reverence and questioned Nārada. ||4||
Indradyumna said:
"My right eye throbs and my left limb trembles; tell me the cause of this, for you alone are a knower of the three periods of time. (5)
Nārada said: O mighty-armed Indradyumna, Hari, whose body is as blue as Indra, has today gone to Pātāla and likewise proceeded to the place called Rohiṇī.
But Indradyumna, having heard those words which were like the falling of a thunderbolt, fell upon the surface of the earth like another peak of a mountain. ||7||
Seeing him fallen upon the ground, all the ministers and priests were distressed and quickly raised the king up.
In the meantime, O Brahmins, Nārada, the foremost of sages,
spoke these pleasing words to the king, whose mind was dejected.
Nārada said:
"I have been sent to your presence by Brahmā; of this there is no doubt.
Now, however, the Lord of the World will establish his abode once again."
When Nārada had spoken thus, O twice-born ones, the people raised a great clamor, crying, "A wooden [image] with a body marked by the conch and discus is floating! (11)
Having heard those words of the people, that king, with a joyful mind, took the ascetic by the hand and stood before him with palms joined in reverence. ||12||
The king said:
"Salutations to you, O Brahmin; salutations to you who hold a lute in your hand.
Having gone and seen [the wood], you have brought back this timber along with the people. (13)
Valabhadra, Jagannātha, Subhadrā, and Sudarśana. ||14||
Hari wears a forest garland and yellow garments, and bears the conch and discus; Balabhadra, endowed with strength, holds a plow and a mace in his hands. ||15||
Having fashioned these images— Subhadrā with a lotus in her hand, and the Sudarśana discus in the form of a pillar— and having installed them here in this pavilion.
The mighty-armed one arrived at the world of Brahmā for the sake of establishing himself;
having gone there, he indeed beheld Brahmā, who bears auspicious marks. (17)
Having bowed down with palms joined in reverence before him, he spoke these words:
"Salutations to you, O Brahman; salutations to you, the Lord of creatures.
Protect me, O abode of compassion; fulfill my heart's desire. (18)
Brahmā said:
"Excellent, O son, O mighty-armed one! A Vaiṣṇava such as you does not exist on earth in the past, nor does he exist now, nor will he ever exist; this is my conviction. (19)
"Now I shall depart for the sake of Cakrapāṇi and perform his consecration; go quickly, O lord of the earth! (20)
Bharadvāja said:
Having heard the words of Brahmā, the king became joyful in mind;
fallen from the world of Brahmā, he entered the world of earth. ||21||
Having arrived there, he beheld the host of that elephant among kings; then, having grappled with him, the lord of kings seized the imperishable Hari.
Then Brahmā descended from the world of Brahmā to the world of the earth;
having arrived swiftly at the earthly realm, he then established his residence there.
With the mantra "Victory is yours," the hosts of deities offered praise;
then the Blessed Lord Hari appeared, bearing the conch and the discus.
Pleased, Viṣṇu spoke this to Indradyumna, the lord of the earth;
the Blessed Lord said:
"O lord of the earth, having abandoned sacred fields and holy fords..."
Right here, indeed, I shall remain with my whole being for a period of a parārdha.
O Indra-dyumna, protector of the earth, listen to my beneficial words:
you should perform the bath and the great festival known as Guḍicā.
Those men who, filled with joy, behold me at the time of my bathing,
being liberated from all sins, go to my own realm.
Having spoken this, the Blessed One Janārdana became silent;
and Brahmā, O best of the twice-born, departed for the world of Brahmā.
For the royal sage Indradyumna, having worshipped the God of gods, the Lord of the universe, with great effort, subsequently attained liberation. ||29||
Thus, O Lord of the World, you who formerly bore the form of Indra-nīla now appear as the Lord of the Universe in the form of the Wooden Brahmā. ||30||
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Attainment of Liberation by King Indradyumna," in the glorious Kapila Purāṇa. ||4||
Now begins the fifth chapter.
Bhāradvāja said:
O best of the twice-born, those men who indeed dwell in that sacred field—
They go to the presence of Viṣṇu, shining with radiant splendor. ||1||
Having bathed in the great ocean and beheld Śrī Puruṣottama, a person shall destroy sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and attain liberation. ||2||
O twice-born ones, whatever fruit one obtains from a pilgrimage to the Gaṅgā, the Sarasvatī, and the Godāvarī, that same fruit one attains simply by beholding the immovable ocean.
And right there is the Mārkaṇḍeya Tīrtha, which purifies the three worlds; having bathed there in ancient times, all the gods attained their own respective abodes. ||4||
O brahmins, the Mārkaṇḍeya-banyan tree was created by Kṛṣṇa himself for the benefit of the great sages and the wise Mārkaṇḍeya. ||5||
Having bathed there and beheld the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain, the best of men shall destroy at that very moment the sins committed throughout ten million births. ||6||
Therefore, O Brahmins, on the Blue Mountain (Nīlācala), to the south of the King of the Gods, there is the one renowned as Yameśvara, who is intent upon the restraint of Yama. ||7||
Having beheld Yameśvara and worshipped him with devotion, a person attains Śiva, being freed from the rod of Yama. ||8||
In its western quarter, there is one known as Alāvunātha;
by taking refuge in him, a person shall attain their heart's desire. ||9||
O protector of the earth, by worshipping that linga, one who is childless becomes possessed of sons, and one who is deformed becomes endowed with the form of the god of love. ||10||
The Liṅga named Kapālamocana is present there; by beholding it with devotion according to the prescribed rite, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa. ||11||
By both eating and seeing it, this place grants liberation to the twice-born;
and there, the twice-born eat well-prepared food and cakes.
Therefore, with every effort, one should go to Puruṣottama;
the Lord of the World should be seen for the sake of one's own liberation. 13.
And at the foot of the banyan tree is Vaṭeśa, the destroyer of all sins;
by the mere sight of him, one is liberated from all sin. ||14||
Indeed, there is no field whatsoever equal to Vārāṇasī; in the entire circle of the three worlds, there is no field equal to that which is called Puruṣa. (15)
And Śrī Puruṣottama is the king of all sacred fields;
Puruṣottama is the supreme among all the gods as well. ||16||
And what is the use of speaking much here again and again?
Truly, truly, truly: there is no field superior to the Supreme Person. (17)
O best of the twice-born, even in hundreds of years one would not be able to describe the majesty of Puruṣottama; what else do you wish to hear? (18)
The sages said:
"You have correctly described the Puruṣottama field that bestows liberation.
O best of the twice-born, tell us what ought to be done in that sacred field."
O Brahmins, it was previously stated by you that Yama is the lord who bestows liberation; all the deities, beginning with Indra, as well as ascetics, reside there.
Even a slight merit performed there becomes equal to Mount Meru; of this there is no doubt.
O Brahmins, perform there penance that bestows liberation.
Bharadvāja said:
That place is exceedingly meritorious and difficult even for the gods and others to attain; by virtue of great merit, both the gods and the great sages reside there. (22)
It was filled with various flowers, adorned with sacrificial posts, and surrounded on all sides by *punnāga* and coconut trees. ||23||
It was filled with *karavīra* and *karṇikāra* trees, as well as *campaka*, *mallikā*, *yūthikā*, and *jāti* flowers.
The great abode of austerity has been proclaimed by the lords of sages;
those men who worship there are peaceful and pure-minded. (25)
By the grace of Yameśvara, they shall attain perfection in mantra;
thus has the majesty of the one named Śrīpuruṣa been recounted by me.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Puruṣottama," in the glorious Kapila Purāṇa.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
The sages said:
"O Brahmins, Kṛṣṇa, Arka, Pārvatī, and Hara were previously described by you."
Now, O Lord, tell us here of the greatness of Bhāskara.
Bharadvāja said:
I shall tell you a secret concerning the most excellent, purifying sacred field,
where in ancient times the brahmins went and Śāmba was liberated from leprosy.
The sages said: From where did Śāmba come? Whom did he propitiate so that he was released? And for what reason did leprosy appear upon his body? Tell us. (3)
Bharadvāja said:
For the sake of subduing the wicked and for the protection of the virtuous, O brahmins, she became renowned as the Śvetagaṅgā in the Kṛṣṇavana forest during the Dvāpara age. 4.
There the Lord, the Master, dwells in the form of Śvetamādhava;
right there is Matsyamādhava, who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
By the conjunction of the sight of both, even an insect may attain liberation. ||5||
The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the slayer of a cow, or even an assassin—
all these attain liberation in the midst of the two white fish.
Having bathed in the Śvetā and beheld the two white fish, a man shall cast off all sins and certainly go to Śvetadvīpa. ||7||
O Brahmins, there is the Indradyumna lake, which was fully honored by Indra; there, a man visibly rejoices together with Indra.
Having seen, bowed to, and worshipped Narasiṃha and Śaṅkara with the blue throat situated there, a person shall go to the world of light (Jyotirloka). ||9||
The man who offers the supreme funeral cake (piṇḍa) between Hari and Śaṅkara, having effected the liberation of his ancestors, shall go to the world of the Sun. ||10||
There, near the Dārubrahma [temple], is the meritorious Kalpavaṭa tree;
by entering its shade, one is liberated even from the sin of killing a Brahmin. ||11||
Hari forgives the faults accumulated over a hundred lifetimes of that person who, having performed a circumambulation, worships that banyan tree.
And at the foot of the Maṅgalāvat tree, having seen and worshipped that goddess who bestows auspiciousness, one is liberated from the bonds of delusion. ||13||
To the west of the banyan tree is Vimalā, the bestower of purity;
by the mere sight of her, a man becomes possessed of knowledge. ||14||
In front of that is Narasiṃha, whose splendor is equal to ten million suns;
the lord of the Daityas also resides there, and he is considered to grant liberation upon being seen. ||15||
In front of him was Vāsudeva, reclining upon Śeṣa, bearing a mace, marked with the conch and discus, and adorned with a forest garland. ||16||
The Lord of the World, who reclines upon the ocean of milk, is personally present here as the Sovereign;
Lakṣmī is at his feet, and Sarasvatī is at the root of his ear. (17)
Above the navel-lotus is Brahmā, who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas; he is the four-armed, four-faced deity holding a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu). ||18||
Since Īśvara, the Lord of Pārvatī, attained the state of being Śeṣa’s body, he, as the non-different Puruṣa, attained oneness. ||19||
Above Acala, the Lord of Gods, known as Puruṣottama, shines forth—the omnipresent one, the manifest Ananta-Puruṣottama himself. ||20||
This sacred field is named Puruṣottama; by beholding the Lord Śrī Śeṣaśāyin here, a person quickly attains liberation. ||21||
In that regard, the remains of offerings made from the wood itself destroy sin, as do the food, cakes, and whatever else is obtained there in abundance. (22)
The food offering of Jagannātha destroys great sins;
by eating it, one obtains the fruit born from the gift of ten million tawny cows.
What merit has he not performed, and what austerity has he not practiced, by whom food was consumed from one who had the very form of a wooden Brahmin? (24)
O twice-born ones, just as Jagannātha certainly grants liberation through direct vision, even so does the food of Jagannātha grant liberation, O brāhmaṇas. 25.
Even though he had gone to another region, Viṣṇu descended; that Lord of the World was drawn forth, surrounded by the gopīs.
Remaining with the cowherds during his childhood, he then slew Kaṃsa;
thereafter, the high-minded Ugrasena was made king in Mathurā.
Out of fear of Kālanemi, he departed from there for the city of Dvārakā;
and Śrī Kṛṣṇa remained there, bestowing welfare upon the Pāṇḍavas. ||28||
Having gone to Hastināpura for Yudhiṣṭhira’s sacrifice of righteousness and having bestowed the white parasol, he returned to the city of Dvārakā. ||29||
O brahmins, as the Lord of the World, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, was thus fleeing, his son Śāmba became the second leader of Rati.
Just like Kṛṣṇa, he too resembles a dark-blue cloud;
his arms are marked with the conch and the discus, he wears yellow garments, and his eyes are beautiful. ||31||
Then that son of Jāmbavatī, delighting in water-sports and surrounded by women, departed unobserved by the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu).
Seeing him, all the women became overwhelmed and fell into a state of infatuation; their seed was discharged, and then Hari uttered a reproach against them.
Fie upon the unchastity of women! Fie, and even more fie!
Seeing their son, how is it that they all fell into delusion again and again? (34)
Then, filled with a slight anger, he spoke to Śāmba.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O dear son, since the semen of the mothers was discharged when you arrived, let leprosy now manifest everywhere upon your body. (36)
When Kṛṣṇa had spoken thus, leprosy appeared on all his limbs; trembling, Śamba also addressed these words to his father. (37)
"O Lord, when an offense has been committed by his son, the father forgives him; what shall I do now? Please tell me how to be released from the curse. (38)
The Blessed One said:
"Having gone to the forest called Maitreya and performed austerities, you, with senses conquered, shall propitiate the Lord of Shade and thereafter attain liberation. (39)
Bharadvāja said:
Having heard these words of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the Lord of Rukmiṇī, Śāmba, overwhelmed with grief, departed immediately all alone. (40)
Having gone there, he practiced most rigorous austerity with great effort—
calm, self-controlled, abstaining from food, subsisting on air alone, and having conquered his senses.
For twelve years, Śāmbo remained devoted to the meditation on the Sun, worshipping, praising, singing, and proclaiming, "Sūrya, Sūrya! ||42||
O Divākara, homage be to you; O Prabhākara, homage be to you. Save me, O abode of compassion, for I am deformed and fallen upon the earth. ||43||
O twice-born ones, praising and singing this mantra, Śāmba, the son of Kṛṣṇa, suddenly fell to the ground, uttering it again and again. (44)
And after some time had passed, the Sun, who is compassionate toward his devotees, spoke these words in a dream regarding the cause for her liberation from the curse: ||45||
The illustrious Sūrya said:
"Stay here, O mighty-armed one; I shall show you my own form.
Having seen it, one is liberated from disease—listen, Śāmbaka, it is not otherwise. (46)
O son of Jāmbavatī, when you desire liberation from evil, recite these names of mine continuously. (47)
The Lord Bhāskara, Sūrya, Citrabhānu, Vibhāvasu, Yamatāta, Aṃśumālin, and the one who bestows affection upon Yamunā. ||48||
The maker of day, the Lord of the world, the witness of all, the dispeller of darkness, the eye of the world, the self-existent, and the bestower of delight through his shadow. ||49||

The enemy of darkness, the sustainer of the planets, the illuminator of the three worlds, the kinsman of devotees, the ocean of compassion, the witness of karma, and the one beyond the supreme. ||50||
Whoever recites these twenty-one names when I have arisen, I grant him peace; I speak the truth, the absolute truth.
Having spoken thus, the Sun departed, and Śāmbo abandoned his sleep;
then, at the time of dawn, he went to the river for the purpose of bathing. ||52||
Having gone there to the highly meritorious Candrabhāgā, which bestows the world of the gods, Sāmba beheld [the goddess] with two arms and marked by the lotus.
He saw an image situated upon a lotus in the midst of the water; having seen that magnificent form, he brought it near with the stream.
Having cleansed her body and washed it with water, the high-minded Śāmba took that image and departed. ||55||
Having caused [the image] to be consecrated with grace, he quickly established it after worshipping it according to the rules with devotion and bowing down most deeply thereafter. ||56||
Freed from disease, he went swiftly to the city of Vārāṇasī.
Bharadvāja said: Thus, in ancient times, Śāmba, having performed austerities and having worshipped the Sun with great effort, was thereby liberated from leprosy.
There, for those most heroic ones who are free from passion and stainless, and who desire to remain [in that state],
may the Blessed Lord Sun fulfill the fruit of their aspirations.
Those who cast off their bodies in the delightful forest named Maitreya go to the world of light, having abandoned all their sins. (60)
Those men who, being composed in mind on a Sunday, behold the Sun with devotion while in the solar asterism, go to the abode of the Sun.
And those who are immortal and free from rebirth in the forest named Maitreya,
having reached the world of the gods, rejoice together with the Sun.
Therein lies the Śrīmaṅgala Tīrtha, which bestows auspiciousness upon the gods; by bathing at Maṅgala, a person will certainly attain auspiciousness. (63)
Therein is the sacred site of Śrīśālmalībhāṇḍa, which purifies the three worlds, removes all sins, is secret, and is frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas. ||64||
It is crowded with various holy men and bestows liberation upon all;
having bathed there, a person shall directly attain the splendor of the sun.
Having bathed in the vessel of the Śrīśālmalī tree and then beheld Chāyāpati,
a person destroys the multitude of their sins and shall dwell in the world of Āditya.
Having bathed in the waters of the Sūryagaṅgā, a person shall go to the world of the Sun;
O brāhmaṇas, there is no sacred ford equal to the Sūryagaṅgā—there is none, there is none! (67)
Having bathed in the great ocean, a person is liberated from all sins;
for this ocean, the lord of rivers, is the best of all sacred bathing places (tīrthas).
Śrī Rāma, for the sake of the welfare of all living beings, worshipped Rāmeśvara right there on the shore of the lord of rivers. (69)
O Brahmins, Rāmacandra bestows their desired boon upon those best of men who worship Rāmeśvara with diligent effort.
O brahmins, those who worship Maheśvara with perfumes, flowers, and food offerings go to the same world as Śiva, resplendent because of that.
Those who bathe there in the waters of the Candrabhāgā according to the prescribed rites,
having assumed bodies equal to the moon, go to the world of the moon.
And there stands a wish-fulfilling tree named Arkavaṭa, crowded with various sages and graced by birds. ||73||

This banyan tree is indeed indestructible and unslayable; it is certainly the bestower of liberation, for the sake of the welfare of all living beings, the Sun himself has manifested as this tree. (74)
There, at the foot of that tree, those who recite the supreme mantra will find that within three fortnights the mantra grants the desired accomplishments of the practitioner. ||75||
O Brahmins, in the world of the Sun at Bhūpāvaṭa, there is what is known as Nandana;
there dwell hosts of Siddhas—I tell you this in truth, truly. (76)
Among them, Viṣṇu is pleased with those who meditate upon Viṣṇu; and those who remain in the shade of the banyan tree become perfected beings (siddhas), of this there is no doubt. ||77||
Those who worship the Sun on the tenth day known as Vijayā,
being liberated from sin, shall achieve victory everywhere.
Those men who, with devotion, witness the great festival of the chariot procession in the meritorious forest named Maitreya, merge into the body of Hari. (79)
O best of the twice-born, there exist such virtues in that most excellent forest named Maitreya; it is not possible to describe them even in hundreds of years.
O Brahmins, I have spoken something that is for your supreme benefit—excellent, most holy; what else do you wish to hear? (81)
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Maitreyavana," in the glorious Kapila Purāṇa. ||6||
Now begins the seventh chapter.
The sages said:
"Now, tell us of the supreme sacred field of Pārvatī."
Through his grace, we shall have our purpose fulfilled; of this there is no doubt. ||1||
Bharadvāja said:
I shall describe the highly meritorious and perfectly pure place called Virajā, which was created of old by Brahmā for the purpose of protecting the creation. 2.
O best of the twice-born, in that sacred field, Virajā bestows freedom from passion; by beholding the face of Virajā, one's worldly impurity is washed away. ||3||
There, the illustrious goddess Virajā, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, remains as Virajā in the Kali age for the benefit of spiritual practitioners. ||4||
Whatever fruit a man obtains by worshipping Hara for ten thousand years, he attains that same fruit simply by beholding Virajā. ||5||
O best of the twice-born, whatever fruit a man obtains at Kurukṣetra or Haridvāra, that same fruit he attains here; it is not otherwise.
The Lord in the form of a boar dwells there as the bestower of liberation;
by seeing and worshipping Him, one shall attain the world of Viṣṇu. ||7||
But there dwells Ākhaṇḍala, the Lord of Pārvatī and teacher of the world; having observed with great effort, he shatters the staff of Yama. ||8||
Where the god Akhaṇḍala resides, there is liberation without a doubt;
having bathed there, they go to the supreme abode of Śrī Viṣṇu. ||9||
Having approached Ākhaṇḍala, a leper is liberated from leprosy, and a woman who is childless shall certainly obtain a son. (10)
O Ākhaṇḍala, salutations to you, the bestower of success upon the perfected ones (siddhas),
the causeless cause of all things, whose form is the unbroken circle.
Whoever beholds the Lord of Pārvatī through this mantra-yoga, being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Śiva. ||12||
Between Kroḍa and Khaṇḍala, in that place difficult for even the gods to attain, even insects and the like go to liberation; how much more so humans who have died there? ||13||

O Brahmins, whether one is a killer of a guru, a killer of a Brāhmaṇa, a killer of a cow, a drinker of liquor, or a reviler of Viṣṇu, by casting off the body there, one certainly attains Vaikuṇṭha. ||14||
There, O Brahmins, is the Muktīśvara Liṅga, which bestows liberation and destroys sin; by those who have seen it, liberation was swiftly attained once again. ||15||
There, in the field of Śrī Viraja, to the northeast of the Goddess, is Gayānābhi, which is highly meritorious and bestows liberation upon the ancestors. (16)
There, those men who, freed from sin, offer a funeral ball (piṇḍa) rescue their ancestors from hell and go to the abode of Hari. ||17||
In that place, O Brahmins, the goddess Vaitaraṇī is a river that bestows liberation; she is indeed the goddess Gaṅgā—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. (18)
The Vaitaraṇī is of great merit, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men; it destroys millions of great sins merely by the sight of its virtuous waters. ||19||

O twice-born ones, having bathed in that [tirtha] and beheld Hari, the giver of prosperity (Śrīdaṃṣṭrin), the best of men shall go to the city of Viṣṇu accompanied by ten million members of his lineage.
Trilocana resides there, the liberator from the sins of worldly existence;
having seen him and worshipped him according to the prescribed rites, one shall attain Trilocana.
O Brahmins, who indeed would not take refuge in that Trilocana, the dispeller of the three-fold afflictions and the presiding lord of the three worlds? (22)
In that excellent field, O Brahmins, is the supreme Kapila-tīrtha, with its clear waters, enchanting and beautiful to behold. (23)
O Brahmins, the husband of the daughter of the Lord of Mountains becomes pleased with that man who bathes at Kāpila on the fourteenth day of the fortnight of the ancestors.
O Brahmins, that man who bathes according to the prescribed rites at the Kāpilika Tīrtha obtains the merit arising from ten million tawny cows; of this there is no doubt. (25)
In that very place is the Gograha Tīrtha, frequented by the lords of sages; having bathed there according to the prescribed rites, one obtains the fruit of Goloka. ||26||
Furthermore, the excellent Somatīrtha exists there, fashioned by the Moon;
having bathed there, O best of men, one goes to the world of the Moon. ||27||
Having enjoyed many pleasures there through the grace of Candra, he certainly becomes a king upon reaching the world of earth. ||28||
Having generated devotion there for Maheśvara, the God of gods, and having abandoned all sin, a person shall go to the city of Viṣṇu. ||29||
Thus, the greatness of Śrī Somatīrtha has been recounted by me;
now, listen as I describe the other sacred fords (tīrthas) today.
O twice-born ones, there exists in that Virajā a place named Kalpāmbusaṃjñaka;
whatever small merit one may have here becomes equal to Mount Meru—of this there is no doubt. (31)
O best of the twice-born, hear what occurred in that field in ancient times:
there was a king named Māndhātṛ, renowned as Satya. ||32||
He was a performer of sacrifices at the best of rituals, a giver of gifts, an enjoyer of pleasures, sweet-spoken, patient by nature, compassionate, truthful in speech, and free from envy. ||33||
This mighty-armed lord of the earth, a scorcher of his enemies, went alone for the sake of hunting into a lonely and dense forest. ||34||
And in a thicket of the forest, he saw a hair-raising python;
seeing it, the wise man struck it down with a single arrow.

And his wife, seeing her husband fallen upon the ground, was overwhelmed with grief and sorrow and uttered this curse upon the king: tasya patnī ca taṃ dṛṣṭvā svapatiṃ patitaṃ bhuvi | duḥkhaśokasamāviṣṭā dadau śāpaṃ nṛpāya tam ||36||
O cruel one, because you have slain my husband, who was as dear to me as life, by means of treachery, therefore, O King, become a jackal. (37)
By the power of her curse, the king turned into a jackal;
having gone there, he spoke these words to the serpent’s wife, who was devoted to her husband.
The king said:
"Tell me quickly how to be released from the curse; save me, for there is no purpose in my living while having assumed the form of a jackal due to the cause of that 'dro' sound. (39)
The wife of the serpent said:
"When you go to the place called Viraja and bathe in that other sacred water (tīrtha), you shall attain liberation. ||40||
O best of kings, the sacred field named Viraja is supremely purifying, delightful, and dispels all sins; it is equal to heaven, without a doubt. (41)
It was filled on all sides by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas;
it was crowded with various hosts of gods and resounded with the beating of divine drums. ||42||
It was adorned with *tittiḍī*, *īśāla*, and *tāla* trees, as well as coconut palms, date palms, mangoes, rose-apples, long peppers, and jackfruit trees.
O King, it is certain that the place named Viraja bestows liberation even upon the wicked;
there alone shall your release from the curse take place. ||44||
Having heard that, the jackal, trembling and deeply distressed, went to Vasiṣṭha’s hermitage and cried out, "Save me! Save me! (45).
Having heard that curse and those words, Vasiṣṭha went outside the hermitage and spoke these pleasing words to him.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Why do you cry out 'Save me'? From where have you come here? What fear has arisen for you? Tell me before me. (47)
Having gone to the forest for the sake of hunting, I, King Māndhātṛ, saw a python there and killed it instantly. (48)
Then, O Sage, I was cursed by his devoted wife, who said:
"Become a jackal once more, because you have killed my husband. (49)
Out of compassion, he spoke again: "Go to the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha;
having gone there, [attain] Śrī Viraja, and through him, liberation will then be obtained. (50)
Now protect me, O Lord; let us go to the stainless realm, O Sage.
Having led me there, quickly deliver me from hell, O Master! (51)
Bharadvāja said:
Having heard those words of his, Vasiṣṭha, filled with compassion and rich in asceticism,
quickly went to that illustrious field of Viraja.
Having gone there, that Lord of Sages diligently bathed him at the sacred ford named Kalpāmbu and bestowed his own body upon him.
And then, O best of the twice-born, having gone from there to his own kingdom, Māndhātṛ beheld a rain of flowers falling from the sky onto the surface of the earth.
And then, O best of the twice-born, Māndhātṛ went to his own kingdom and protected his subjects with righteousness and discipline.
Then the highly effulgent Vasiṣṭha, surrounded by his disciples,
went to that delightful hermitage of his own, which was composed entirely of merit.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, I have heard all that occurred in the past at that sacred ford known as Kalpāmbu, which destroys every sin. (57)
"O twice-born ones, though his merit was small, it will become vast like the waters of the kalpa;
thus the king, having abandoned his jackal state, was liberated. (58)
Whoever should recite this meritorious and great narrative that removes sin, or even listen to it with diligence, attains a meritorious destination. ||59||
Having heard this, may all people always pay homage to the serpent;
for Māndhātṛ, having slain a serpent, indeed attained such a destination.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Release of Śṛgāla," in the glorious Kapila Purāṇa. ||7||
Now begins the eighth chapter.
The sages said:
We have heard with reverence the greatness of Alpāmbu-tīrtha.
In this regard, O Sage, we desire to hear about the secret sacred fords.
Bharadvāja said:
There is a sacred ford there named Mṛtyuñjaya, praised by the hosts of gods, where the son of Mṛkaṇḍu, having bathed, conquered death. (2)
That man who performs an ablution at Mṛtyuñjaya, the most excellent of holy sites, and beholds Mṛtyuñjaya himself, shall likewise seek to conquer death. (3)
And there lies the Kroḍatīrtha, supremely purifying and great;
the Lord of the World, in the form of a boar, has himself become the very embodiment of the sacred ford. ||4||
Having quickly performed his ablutions there, he should recite the mantra "And he dissolves into the body of the boar," and thus meditate upon the Lord Mṛtyuñjaya. ||5||
O King of Holy Places, salutations to you; O you who are flooded with the waters of compassion, lift me up from the flood of sins as I sink down; protect me, O Lord! (6)
Right there is Śukatīrtha, which bestows the state of Vāsudeva; having bathed there even once, a person shall go beyond the world of the gods.
Having thus praised the sacred ford named Siddheśvara, which bestows perfection and grants all desires, and having drunk the water, the perfected ones attained the state of perfection. ||8||
O twice-born ones, when the head is offered even once at Siddheśvara,
the Lord of Creatures, being pleased, shall grant him whatever success he desires.
Whoever has bathed for even a single day at the beautiful Siddheśvara, where the waters are clear and auspicious, has effectively bathed throughout the three worlds. (10)
Such is the manifold merit of that Siddheśvara;
and by bathing at Siddheśvara, a person attains perfection without a doubt. ||11||
O best of the twice-born, there are various sacred fords (tīrthas) there, as well as various deities and various hosts of perfected beings (siddhas). ||12||
That best of men who travels to Virajā-kṣetra during the month of Madhu, or indeed during Āśvina or Mādhava, shall certainly attain perfection. (13)
Those men who behold the place of the swing and the lap there have attained liberation after destroying sins such as the killing of a Brahmin. ||14||
On a Tuesday or on a Thursday, whoever beholds Viraja with devotion shall attain devotion. ||15||
In that regard, O best of the twice-born, it is the truth, the absolute truth, that the supreme mantra which one recites at the peak of Śrīviraja shall grant him success. (16)
One who constantly worships the Lord born of the ocean on its back—either upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), in an image, or in an auspicious śālagrāma stone—[attains the highest state]. ||17||
One should worship Janārdana with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, incense, lamps, hymns, as well as with garlands or betel leaves. 18.
Within six months, the deity grants the desired boon;
having attained perfection, and upon death, one indeed goes to the stainless Viṣṇu.
O best of beings, who among embodied souls is able to describe these stainless qualities of this one named Viraja, except for Śeṣa? (20)
And for that auspicious person who recites the Virajā mantra at the end of a thousand yojanas, it is said that the goddess, being devoted to him, grants whatever he desires. 21.
O best of the twice-born, thus has that place named Viraja been described by me;
having performed penance there, you shall attain supreme perfection. ||22||
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Girijā," in the glorious Kapila Purāṇa. ||8||
Now begins the ninth chapter.
The sages said:
"Previously, Kṛṣṇa, Arka, Pārvatī, and Hara were described by you."
Now we desire to hear; O Śambhu, speak to us.
O Brahmin, you have described that Puruṣottama which bestows liberation, known as Maitreya and Viraja, and which destroys all sins. ||2||
The mountain Nīlādri is covered with water; beyond that is the one called Viraja, which is even more so;
and Maitreya is strewn with sand and difficult to endure due to the heat of the sun.
Therefore, O you whose wealth is austerity, there is nothing more supremely purifying than this; tell us, O Lord, of that mountain which is a field for our ascetic practice. (4)
"You previously stated that Viśveśvara resides there; tell us his location, for that alone shall be the fruit of our penance. (5)
Bharadvāja said:
O best of the twice-born, I shall describe the supremely meritorious abode of Śambhu,
the delightful Kailāsa, the foremost of mountains, which removes all sins.
O twice-born ones, Kailāśa is heard of as being between Virajā and Ekāmra; there resides the god Śrīśikhareśvara, who removes all sins. ||7||
It was adorned with *vakula* and *campaka* trees in full bloom, as well as with mangoes, betel-nut trees, and coconut palms, all bearing young shoots and accompanied by celestial beings. ||8||
With date palms and arjuna trees, with beautiful jackfruit trees, and with karkandhu, kulaka, and lovely-looking pomegranate trees. ||9||
With bilva, lodhra, and palāśa trees, with punnāgas, tuṅgas, and keśaras, with jambu, dantaśaṭa, and kovidāra trees laden with fruit. ||10||
And with tamarind and vaṭa trees, as well as khadira, campaka, pāribhadra, bakula, dhātrī, and nāgakeśara trees. ||11||
And with *jātī*, *kājūthikā*, and well-scented flowers, as well as with *tagara*, *mallikā*, *karavīra*, and *pāṭala* blossoms. ||12||
With *aśoka* trees, *mālatī* jasmine, *mādhavī* creepers, clusters of *kadamba*, *sevantikā* flowers, *kunda* blossoms, and golden *kāñcana* flowers—both white and red. ||13||
Thus, that abode of Viśvanātha was indeed filled on all sides with various kinds of trees, flowers, and diverse men. ||14||
Having approached Śikhareśa, he who takes refuge in him with the mantra for a year without sloth—his mantra becomes successful. ||15||
Therein, that Viśvanātha, devoted to the creation of the universe, is the glorious bestower of liberation and the fulfillment of desires in the form of a Liṅga; of this there is no doubt. (16)
Having abandoned numerous fields of merit and sacred sites,
the Lord of Pārvatī, the scorcher of foes, remains alone on Kailāsa.
When Kailāsa was lifted up by the evil-minded Rāvaṇa, that single peak fell; therefore, it is called Kailāśa here. ||18||
I consider Kailāśa to be superior, because it is situated in the land of action; there the fruit of action is experienced, whereas there [on Kailāśa] there is only enjoyment. (19)
For those best of men who dwell on Kailāśa, the abode of Śaṅkara, the attainment of the fruits of enjoyment in this world and liberation itself are held within their hands. 20.
It is the abode of Śambhu on Mount Kailāśa, difficult to attain and bestowing liberation, where hosts of gods dwell eternally in the presence of Śambhu. ||21||

Having beheld the Lord of the Peaks (Śikhareśa), worshipped him, and prostrated before him, a person should cast away the fault of smelling flowers from a cow, offer the arghya water, and then proceed. ||22||

Remembering that Śikhareśvara is indeed the cause of destruction, one should quickly go there to atone for the offense committed against the guru’s wife as well as for any disparagement of the guru. (23)
All the deities, beginning with Brahmā, repeatedly long for this:
"When, having gone to the world of mortals, shall we behold Śikhareśvara? (24)
Both the ancestors and the subjects long for a good king, such as one who, born in our lineage, shall go to Mount Kailāsa. (25)
Having gone there with diligence, he shall bathe in that sacred ford of milk and nectar, and after offering libations to us, he will deliver us from hell. ||26||
O best of the twice-born, on that mountain there is a sacred ford called Payo'mṛta, situated in the northeastern direction in front of Śrīśikhareśa. ||27||
It is most excellent, supremely meritorious, and bestows liberation upon the ancestors;
having bathed there, King Saudāsa indeed attained liberation.
The sages said:
O best of the twice-born, tell us in detail the greatness of that sacred ford, as well as the greatness of other sacred fords on that mountain.
Bhāradvāja said:
"In Bhogavatī, on the earth, in the heavenly realm, and throughout the world of moving and non-moving beings, there is no sacred ford equal to milk-nectar; I say, there is none, truly none."
In former times, in the Satya age, there was a lord of the earth named Saudāsa in the solar dynasty; he was a tiger among men, devoted to the protection of his subjects. (31)
He was a speaker and a listener, profoundly peaceful like another Bṛhaspati;
in form he was the Lord of Rati, yet in battle he was the leader of the Śacīs.
The thought arose in him to accomplish a mantra;
the king questioned Vasiṣṭha, who was standing before him in his own city. (33)
Saudāsa said:
"O best of beings, tell me where the perfection of mantra may be attained;
having bathed and recited there, I shall go to the supreme state. (34)
There lies the sacred field of Vārāṇasī, which bestows liberation and grants the desires of spiritual perfection, where the Lord Viśveśvara resides, granting boons to practitioners. (35)
O King, there is no sacred field on the surface of the earth equal to Vārāṇasī, where the Lord of the Universe himself resides in person, assuming the form of a Liṅga. (36)
O protector of the earth, in that field there is the sacred site of Śrī Maṇikarṇikā;
by bathing there, a man or a woman is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
There the holy Bhāgīrathī, which bestows liberation upon men, is established in the world of mortals, in Pātāla, and in the heavenly realm. ||38||
The greatness of the Bhāgīrathī has been described in detail from of old;
even a mere drop of its water can bring about the destruction of the sin of killing a Brahmin. (39)
O King, Vārāṇasī, Viśvanātha, the Gaṅgā, and Maṇikarṇikā—each one alone is difficult to attain; how much more so where all four are present? (40)
Bharadvāja said:
Having heard these words of the great seer, O lord of men, the king prostrated before that ṛṣi and quickly set out for that supreme field.
Having gone and bathed in the Gaṅgā and beheld the Lord of Pārvatī, he,
endowed with forgiveness and truth, performed most rigorous penance.
And when some time had passed in this manner, the god Maheśvara,
having revealed his true form, spoke these words to him in a dream.
Śaṅkara said:
O mighty-armed one, you have come to my field that bestows liberation;
now go to my abode on Kailāsa for the sake of penance.
There I shall show you my true form;
I shall grant you liberation as well. This which I have spoken is the truth, the absolute truth.
And right beside me, O Indra of the gods, is the sacred ford named Payo'mṛta, which bestows the four aims of human existence; there, I am Śikhareśvara. (46)
The Liṅga named Śrīśikhareśvara removes all sins;
to whoever beholds me stationed there, I grant liberation. ||47||
O lord of the earth, being pleased by his penance there in the Kṛta Yuga,
he himself became the bestower of perfection through his very sight in the Tretā and Dvāpara ages.
And in the Kali age, I am indeed the bestower of perfection upon men merely by being seen;
moreover, he who bathes in that excellent sacred ford, the Amṛta-paya, on that mountain—[attains success]. 49.
He goes to the supreme abode and dissolves into my body; in the great sacred ford of nectar, his water becomes like nectar itself. ||50||
"Bestow immortality quickly once the bath has been performed in your waters;
O King, perform the bathing there according to this rite. (51)
Having bathed there and beheld me, you shall attain supreme perfection; right there is an excellent sacred ford in my presence that destroys all sins.
Known as Jambhakunu, a certain peak stands at the front;
there the waters fall, bestowing auspiciousness upon all limbs, purifying all worlds, and bringing welfare to all the world. (53)
Having bathed there in the waters cool from the mountain, that best of men, having placed his head in the water and become purified, shall obtain happiness. (54)
O descendant of the solar dynasty, listen to the merit that comes from bathing there: having bathed well in the Kailāśa-kunda and worshipped Maheśvara. (55)
A person attains perfection through his grace; of this there is no doubt.
For I am present, indeed, in that water and at my sacred ford (tīrtha), where I am to be worshipped. 56.
"Having gone there, one attains the state of liberation through the recitation of mantras";
having said this, the Lord departed, and then the king awoke from his sleep.
And the illustrious king went alone to the supreme Mount Kailāśa; having bathed there in the Payo'mṛta tīrtha, the king performed austerities. (58)
Having remained there for some time, that Lord of the gods of gods subsequently attained liberation, alone upon that Mount Kailāsa.
Having raised a clamor there, one is certainly cooked in hell;
thus have I declared that supreme mountain to be that place.
Having gone there and performed austerities, you two shall attain the highest perfection.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Attainment of Liberation by Saudāsa," in the glorious Kapila Purāṇa. ||9||
Now begins the tenth chapter.
The sages said:
"By creating a clamor there, a man enters hell."
"We shall go there; tell us how, Bharadvāja. (1)
You have correctly described Kailāśa, the abode of the Lord of Pārvatī, as a great place for performing penance—a site that is entirely free from defects. (2)
O ascetic, O best of the twice-born, there is another sacred field in Utkala; out of a desire for our welfare, please tell us about it quickly. (3)
O best of sages, through your grace we shall have our purpose fulfilled;
O high-minded one, what other secret remains? Speak it quickly.
Bharadvāja said:
"O best of sages, having become one-pointed in mind, listen;
this which was previously told to someone must be guarded with great effort. (5)

O you whose wealth is penance, on that mountain there is known a practice called "the making of one-pointedness," which is to be understood as the most secret of secrets and is remembered as higher than the highest. (6)
This sacred field, which bestows liberation upon living beings, increases the victory of the gods, is stainless and formless, and has the nature of both Hari and Hara. (7)
It was crowded with hosts of perfected men (siddhas), graced by the lords of sages, and frequented by gandharvas, kinnaras, vidyādharas, and cāraṇas. ||8||
And with mango, nimba, and kadamba trees, all in bloom and laden with fruit, as well as with betel-nut trees, jackfruit trees, banyans, and bakula trees. ||9||
With *palāśa*, *mucukunda*, and *pārijāta* trees, with *priyaṅgu*, *karkandhu*, *nāgaraṅga*, and even *rājādana* trees. ||10||
And with *khadira*, *vilva*, *vañcu*, *karahāṭaka*, *karṇikāra*, *japā* flowers, *kapittha*, and *cipumaṇdaka* trees. ||11||
With *campaka*, *atimukta*, and well-blossomed *nāgakeśara* flowers;
with *śāla*, *tāla*, and *śirīṣa* trees; and with *jambīra* trees that are pleasant to behold. ||12||
It was filled with most enchanting groves of plantain trees, as well as with abundant and excellent *karavīra*, *kaṇikāra*, and *kapittha* trees. (13)
And with *yūthikā* and *mallikā* flowers, as well as *jātī*, *lakucaka*, *aśoka*, and *vakuula* trees, which were graced by swarms of bees. ||14||
O twice-born ones, that forest was filled with various kinds of trees, such as *mālatī* creepers, pomegranates, and citron trees. (15)
With cuckoos of ten-fold gait and crooked gait, sweetly warbling, as well as sparrows, *cātakas*, *cakoras*, and birds of variegated plumage; ||16||
O fair-faced one, there were also tigers, cocks adorned with crests upon their heads, pigeons with delicate wings, and those with backs like iron.
With female and male swans, as well as with parrots joined by their mates, with quails, partridges, and peacocks performing intense dances; ||18||
With lions, tigers, rhinoceroses, wild boars, langurs, deer, and likewise with various other kinds of quadrupeds and birds. ||19||
That meritorious grove was filled with oblong ponds and lakes, adorned with lotuses and water lilies, and perfected by birds of their own kind.
It was graced with kāraṇḍava ducks, water-fowls, swans, clusters of lotuses, and water-hens;
its waters were free from mud and transparent, and it shone with flights of steps.
Thus, this great forest, beloved by Viṣṇu, is completely filled on all sides with various kinds of virtues; it is singularly focused and supremely meritorious.
It was cool and most enchanting, with its holy waves that were fragrant, heavy, and restless, tossed by the leftward wind.
O best of sages, know this to be the manifest realm of Vaikuṇṭha;
for there, the Lord of the World shines with a body as dark as a blue stone, amidst one-pointed devotion.
There dwells the glorious Lord of the Universe, Śambhu, who bears the conch and the discus, is adorned with a forest garland, and is manifestly of the nature of Nārāyaṇa. (25)
Since you desire liberation, therefore indeed go there.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of Ekāmra," in the glorious Kapila Purāṇa.
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
The sages said:
"O Sage, describe in detail the sacred field of Ekāmra."
And there are delightful hermitages and tens of millions of lingas there. ||1||
All of us, desiring to hear this, shall go without a doubt;
we shall worship Virūpākṣa Janārdana, who has the luster of a water-bearing cloud.
Bharadvāja said:
The glorious field of Ekāmra bestows supreme bliss; for a distance of one krośa on all sides, the earth is covered with ten million liṅgas.

There, that God of gods, the Lord of Pārvatī, accompanied by his own attendants, is the bestower of boons upon men, the giver of liberation, and the granter of perfection to spiritual practitioners. ||4||
The Supreme Lord, established in the form of supreme bliss, should be known as higher than the highest, the bestower of boons upon Brahmā and the other gods. ||5||
Having abandoned Vārāṇasī, Maheśvara, surrounded by water, requested the merit of Hari and entered the Ekāmra forest. ||6||
The sages said:
"O Lord, tell us in detail this entire account: when was this requested by Śambhu in the form of the Liṅga?"
Bharadvāja said: O brahmins, formerly in the Tretā Yuga, while staying in Vārāṇasī, Maheśvara spoke these words to Nārada, the bull among sages.
Śiva said: "O sage, by presiding over this city, the sin of a man is destroyed; yet once it has become crowded with people, it will cause obstacles to ascetic practice."
It is not proper to remain in a place crowded with people;
for there, one may encounter disturbances caused by atheists who are weak in knowledge. (10)
O lords of sages, where atheists reside, there dharma is not found; and because of that unrighteousness, the portion belonging to Hari becomes lost.
This place was formerly prepared with great effort for the sake of Pārvatī; it is a beautiful spot where Pārvatī dwelt, and which brings me joy. (12)
O best of sages, my mind no longer finds the strength to remain here;
tell me quickly, where is that supreme secret place? (13)
Nārada said:
On the shore of the salt ocean stands Līlaśaila, the best of mountains;
to its north, O Lord, is the famous sacred field of Ekāmraka.
There, the glorious Vāsudeva, the Lord of Ramā and the Teacher of the World, remained alone with Ananta in the solitary forest. (15)
That supreme, secret place Prajāpati does not know;
even the Blessed One knows it—what then can be said of the gods?
The supreme secret of Ekāmra belongs to the Lord of the World who wields the discus;
even the Daughter of the Ocean, seated upon his lap, does not know it, nor does Śaṅkara. ||17||
There, Janārdana himself is present in person along with Ananta; by him, the creation, destruction, and maintenance of the world are deliberated.
He too, Lakṣmaṇa, is always infinite; he remains with the Lord, as does Rāmacandra and Kṛṣṇa, the son of Rohiṇī. ||19||
Having performed penance for many days, Maheśvara and Vāsudeva became pleased, and they recognized that place as the most excellent sacred field.
I am Śeṣa, the Lord of the World; therein lies the union of the three, which does not exist among Indra and the other gods, nor among others. ||21||
Thus, O Lord, that supreme merit was known by me in the past;
now this most sacred field has been known by you.
Bharadvāja said:
When this had been thus spoken by Nārada, the Lord of Caṇḍikā then placed his hand in the hand of the sage and set his mind upon departing. 23.
He spoke these words to Nandikeśvara, the leader of the Gaṇas: "I shall go to Ekāmraka; prepare yourself, my son."
"Take the bull-king and go quickly to the auspicious daughter of the mountain.
Having received the Lord's command upon his head, the wielder of the trident then departed.
Having brought Vṛṣabha, Pārvatī went forth and quickly recounted the ten million liṅgas according to their respective numbers.
"Prepare yourselves; the Teacher of the World has gone to Gataikāmra," he said, and taking Girijā upon his bull, he departed for that place.
Having himself assumed the guise of a courtesan, the God of gods ascended [the chariot] which resembled ten million moons and was adorned with various ornaments. ||28||
Having seen his own vehicle, Śambhu praised Nandin; then that Lord of Nandin [placed his hands] upon the ears of the God of gods.
He put on an earring adorned with various jewels,
shining like ten million suns and as pure as gold and lapis lazuli.
On the region of the head, there is a beautiful crown adorned with a crescent moon, along with pure, well-perfumed sandalwood mixed with camphor. ||31||
Then she applied cool sandalwood paste upon the forehead of the Lord of Pārvatī, and likewise saffron and the deer-design upon his cheeks.
Nandi quickly gave her pure betel-leaf for her lips,
and likewise a radiant necklace of rubies and pearls for her heart.
He dyed the sandalwood paste with lead, the flower garland with lac, and the two shining golden bracelets with rubies.
Upon his two shoulders, which were like the sun and moon, he placed lightning-like crescent moons;
there, upon his waist, was a silk garment, and above that, a cloth for the girdle.
She adorned herself with a girdle beautifully embellished with tiny bells, and placed upon her feet divine anklets set with blue sapphires.
Thus Nandikeśa made the Lord well-attired;
well-dressed, with a gracious countenance, and glorious, Hara possessed the luster of ten million moons. ||37||
The Lord, together with Vṛṣa, having placed the daughter of the Himālaya on his lap, thus assumed this form and departed quickly while being praised by those walking before him. ||38||
With white yak-tail fans and whisks, and with white parasols held over his head by Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras—parasols that put to shame the brilliance of ten million suns. (39)
The hosts of apsarases perform long-sounding, very extensive, and delightful dances with knitted brows, as well as dances accompanied by shouts of victory. (40)
Holding a trident and a hand-drum, and clad in tiger-skin garments, thus is the illustrious Lord of Pārvatī, the bestower of boons upon his devotees. ||41||
Having been led to Ekāmra by the high-souled Nārada,
he went to that place and, with self-restraint, prostrated himself before the eternal Vāsudeva with all eight limbs and quickly offered this hymn of praise.
The illustrious Śaṅkara said: Salutations to you, O Supreme Bliss; salutations to you whose eyes are blue-black; salutations to you, Hari, who bears the form of the three Vedas.
Salutations to you whose body has become blue; O Leader of the World, you are the bestower of boons upon the gods, the remover of distress for those who are devoted, O Lord! (44)
Salutations to you who dwell in Ekāmra, who are clothed in yellow garments, whose external form consists of the three qualities (guṇas), and who bear the conch and the discus. ||45||
You alone are the origin of the worlds and the cause of all causes;
O friend of devotees, Lord of the universe, ocean of compassion! 46.
O Lord, you have thousands of delightful abodes; yet, O Master, I do not know how it is that you remain in a hidden form at Ekāmra.
O Viṣṇu, he said to me in the past: "You are half of my body;
but now, O Keśava, how is it that you have ruled the kingdom? (48)
Nārada is your devotee, and the Lord of Serpents is your bed; for they two alone know you, O Lord—there is no mercy shown to me. (49)
O Lord, devotion has been granted by you to the gopīs who are devoted with love;
yet Sanaka and the others remain [detached], for the will of the Lord is unrestrained. (50)
O Supreme Lord, they remain in the delightful forest of Ekāmra,
having resorted to yogic sleep, with their two eyes sealed.
Now, O Lord of the World, having shown compassion, grant me my own place; I have come into your presence to abide there. (52)
While the Lord of the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain was thus offering praise,
Viṣṇu opened his eyes and, smiling, spoke these words.
Śrī Vāsudeva said:
Listen to my words, O Śambhu; I shall speak what is for your benefit.
I will grant you a place to dwell; make a promise of truth before me. (54)
"I shall never remain here forever, surrounded by my own attendants for the sake of dwelling in Kāśī; this is the truth, O Maheśvara. (55)
The illustrious Śaṅkara said:
"How could I not go to Kāśī? There dwells for me the holy Jāhnavī, who embodies all sacred fords; there is my sacred ford, Maṇikarṇikā. (56)
Vāsudeva said:
"O Lord of the Mountain, neither Nārada nor Śeṣa knows this; I alone know it—know this now, O Hara. (57)
Right here is the auspicious Jāhnavī, which flows from the tip of my foot;
and in the south-eastern direction on my back is the Gaṅgā known as Munisaṃjñakā.
"O Śaṅkara, there are other well-concealed sacred fords belonging to me; I shall tell you all of them later. Now, fulfill the truth."
Śaṅkara said:
"It is the truth, the absolute truth that I declare here: O Madhusūdana, I shall not leave Vārāṇasī for other sacred sites, O Mādhava."
O Lord, I shall remain in the Ekāmra forest in your presence;
truly, truly, again truly, I shall not go anywhere else. (61)
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Śambhu, assuming the form of the quarter, remains in the southern direction of that Viṣṇu, bestowing the fruits of the four aims of life.
The Linga, the Lord of the Three Worlds, is like crystal at its base, deep blue in the middle, and like a ruby at its tip. 63.
Bhāradvāja said:
From that time forth, O Brahmins, the illustrious King Maheśvara remained in the field surrounded by ten million liṅgas, while Vāsudeva was the protector. ||64||
Those best of sages who behold his linga at Ekāmra—whether they have committed ten thousand killings of Brahmins or not—liberation stands within their grasp. (65)
Having thus entreated the eternal Vāsudeva, the Lord Śambhu remained in the forest of Ekāmra, bearing ten million liṅgas.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Arrival of Maheśa at Ekāmra," in the glorious Kapila Purāṇa. ||11||
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
The sages said:
O best of the twice-born, tell us of a merit-bestowing sacred site (tīrtha) located at that very place.
Thus the name arose, well-guarded by the wielder of the discus.
Bharadvāja said:
After some time had passed, the god Maheśvara remained there sporting; as he stayed there, a certain visible form came into being. ||2||
And at that moment, O Brahmins, drops of water flowed forth;
therefore, the hosts of gods together gave it the name Bindusaras (the Lake of Drops). ||3||
One should worship all the sacred fords beginning with Puṣkara, the oceans beginning with the Ocean of Milk, the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, and indeed all the gods. ||4||
All [the rivers] there flowed drops of water day and night;
therefore, in the Veda and the Purāṇa, it is known by the name Vindusarovara. ||5||
The Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, Revā, Tuṅgabhadrā, Narmadā, Kālindī, Sarayū, and Tāpī flow there as well. ||6||
O twice-born ones, Mānasa, Puṣkara, Pampā, Sutīkṣṇa, and Śailanirmala— all these flow into the sacred ford of Vindūdbhava.
In the sacred ford known as Vindūdbhava, there exist the oceans of milk, salt, water, and indeed curd, as well as oceans of clarified butter and wine.
And that sacred site is at Dvāravatī, in Naimiṣa, in the Daṇḍaka forest,
at Vindūdbhava, and likewise eternally at Badarikāśrama.
O Brahmins, it is heard that there is a sacred ford called Bindusaras in the Ekāmraka forest;
having bathed and drunk there, a man shall not go to hell.
O Brahmins, there is the sacred ford known as Vindūdbhava, frequented by the lords of sages, which is pure with stainless water and adorned with steps. ||11||

In heaven, on earth, in the netherworld, as well as in the atmosphere and in every direction, there has been no sacred site (tīrtha) nor will there ever be one superior to that which originated from the Bindu. 12.
O Brahmins, the water produced from the drops is nectar; of this there is no doubt.
Having bathed in the Vindūdbhava, the man who beholds the Bull-bannered Lord [Śiva], [attains the highest state]. 13.
Freed from all sins, one is absorbed into the body of Śiva;
and here indeed, O best of the twice-born, the goddess known as Pādaharā is heard of.
